newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan mulls BOJ, private bank aid to NCB - sources.
newsitem.headline: Japan mulls BOJ, private bank aid to NCB - sources.

text.p: The Bank of Japan (BOJ) is mulling channelling 80 billion yen to Nippon Credit Bank Ltd through a special fund originally designed to deal with bad loans at the nation's failed "jusen" mortgage firms, banking sources said on Friday.
The planned BOJ fund is likely to be used to buy NCB preferred shares, the banking sources said.

Japanese financial authorities are also considering asking major Japanese private banks to provide about 70 billion yen to buy new NCB ordinary shares in order to help the troubled bank restructure itself to cope with its bad loans, the sources said.
Life insurers may also be asked by the authorities to extend subordinated loans to NCB that could total about 150 billion yen, they added.
Through these measures, NCB is likely to get financial support totalling some 300 billion yen, which would help the bank strengthen its financial base, the sources said.

A condition of the financial support from Japanese private banks is likely to be that it would only be given if NCB posts a net loss in the financial year ending March 31 for the second consecutive year, which would hurt its capital base, they said.
A senior BOJ official said meanwhile that the central bank would probably draw up plans to support NCB after NCB presents a sweeping restructuring plan to the Japanese authorities.
"If we are to support the bank, we will provide money through" the special jusen fund, the official told Reuters.

Asked whether the BOJ money would be used to purchase NCB preferred shares, the official said: "That's likely at the moment, but I cannot comment on any details of possible support from the BOJ and the Ministry of Finance before NCB unveils its own restructuring plan."
On Thursday, NCB said it would announce a restructuring plan in early April.
Tadao Iwaki, a senior managing director at NCB, told reporters that the bank had to see its final earnings results for 1996/97 before officially deciding on its restructuring plan.

Although Iwaki declined to elaborate on details of the bank's reform plan, as it has not been officially decided, he said sales of real estate and the closure of some branches were among measures which would likely be considered.
